  The components of a fitted model, what the printed summary says line by
  line, importance, plots with glex, and how a component of three predictors
  is shown.
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 3.5,
  out.width = "100%"
)
```

A model fitted by `rpf()` is a sum of a few functions, the components, each of one, two or three predictors.
This article shows how to read them: from the printed summary, as numbers from `predict_components()`, and as plots.
It uses simulated data, so that we can compare every component with the truth.

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(randomPlantedForest)
library(glex)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
```

## Data with known components

The outcome is a sum of four terms: two main effects, a two-way and a three-way interaction.
`x5` has no effect.

$$y = \sin(\pi x_1) + x_2 + 2 x_1 x_3 + 3 x_2 x_3 x_4 + \varepsilon$$

```{r simulate}
set.seed(2)
n <- 2000
sim <- data.frame(
  x1 = runif(n, -1, 1),
  x2 = runif(n, -1, 1),
  x3 = runif(n, -1, 1),
  x4 = runif(n, -1, 1),
  x5 = runif(n, -1, 1)
)
sim$y <- sin(pi * sim$x1) + sim$x2 + 2 * sim$x1 * sim$x3 +
  3 * sim$x2 * sim$x3 * sim$x4 + rnorm(n, sd = 0.3)
```

The predictors are independent and uniform on [-1, 1], so each term has mean zero, and the interactions have mean zero along each of their predictors.
These are the conditions under which the four terms are exactly the components the model estimates (see "Purification" below).

```{r fit}
model <- rpf(y ~ ., data = sim, nthreads = 2)
```

## The printed summary, line by line

```{r print}
model
```

- **`Regression. Prediction = intercept + the sum of 4 components.`** The kind of model, and how many components it has.
  The prediction for a row is exactly this sum.
- **`Intercept`**: the constant part, here close to the true value 0.
- **The component table** lists the components, largest first.
  The importance of a component is its share of the variance of the model's prediction on the training rows (the column `model_share` of `model$components`).
  The shares need not add up to 100%: the components are not uncorrelated on the data.
  Here the model found the four true terms, and no other.
- **`How it was chosen`** summarises the three steps of the default call:
  - **`The forest`**: how many tree families were grown, and how many splits each made.
    The number of splits was chosen out of bag while the forest grew, and growing stopped a little later, once more splits no longer helped.
    See [The number of splits and further tuning](number-of-splits-and-tuning.html).
  - **`From the forest's ... nonzero components`**: the forest itself has many more components than the model.
    Pruning kept those with a share of at least `tau` of the variance of the forest's prediction, and with rule R refitted one coefficient per kept component.
  - **`Rule and threshold chosen by out-of-bag error`**: the rule (D or R) and `tau` were chosen out of bag, with the 1-SE rule, among 16 candidates.
  - **`Left out`**: the components that were dropped, with their shares added up.
    Here they are small, and the true model has none of them.
  - **`Components of three or more predictors in at most 10 heat maps each`** and **`Heat-map forms`**: how the three-way component is shown (see "Components of three predictors" below).

[Pruning to a sparse model](pruning.html) explains the rules and the threshold.

## The components as numbers

`predict_components()` evaluates every component of the model at the rows of `new_data`:

```{r components}
comp <- predict_components(model, new_data = sim)
comp$intercept
head(comp$m)
```

`m` has one column per component.
Each column is that component's contribution to the prediction of the row, on the scale of the outcome, and the intercept and the columns add up to the prediction:

```{r components-sum}
all.equal(comp$intercept + rowSums(comp$m), predict(model, sim)$.pred)
```

So a single prediction can be read as a sum.
For the first row:

```{r one-row}
round(unlist(c(intercept = comp$intercept, comp$m[1, ])), 3)
predict(model, sim[1, ])
```

`predict_components()` takes new data as `predict()` does, and `predictors` restricts it to the components of some predictors (the others are returned as one `remainder` column, so that the sum still holds).

## Importance

`model$components` has one row per component the model considered:

```{r components-table}
model$components[, c("component", "order", "share", "kept", "beta", "model_share")]
```

- `share` is the component's share of the variance of the forest's prediction, before pruning.
  It is what the threshold `tau` is compared with.
- `beta` is the coefficient rule R fitted to the component.
- `model_share` is the share of `beta` times the component in the model's prediction: the importance that `print()` shows.

```{r three-way-numbers, include = FALSE}
three <- model$components[model$components$component == "x2:x3:x4", ]
```

The forest shrinks interactions: it averages many tree families, and some of them never find a given interaction.
The refit of rule R restores their size.
Here it multiplies the three-way component by `r round(three$beta, 2)`, and the component's importance is `r round(100 * three$model_share)`% of the model where its `share` of the forest was `r round(100 * three$share)`%.

glex has another measure, the mean absolute contribution of each component over the rows:

```{r vi, fig.alt = "Bar chart of the mean absolute contribution of each of the four components.", fig.height = 3}
autoplot(glex_vi(comp))
```

The two measures need not give the same order.
The variance weights large contributions more than the mean absolute value does, so a component that is large on a few rows, such as an interaction that is large only where all its predictors are far from 0, ranks higher by variance.

## Plots with glex

`predict_components()` returns an object of class `glex`, which the [glex](https://plantedml.com/glex/) package draws with `autoplot()`.
A main effect is a curve; a two-way interaction is a scatter of the data coloured by the component's value.

Here the true main effects are added as orange lines:

```{r main-effects, fig.alt = "The estimated main effects of x1 and x2 as step curves, with the true functions drawn over them."}
truth <- data.frame(x = seq(-1, 1, length.out = 200))
add_truth <- function(p, f) {
  p + geom_line(aes(x, y), data = transform(truth, y = f(x)), inherit.aes = FALSE,
                colour = "orange", linewidth = 0.8)
}
add_truth(autoplot(comp, "x1"), function(x) sin(pi * x)) +
  add_truth(autoplot(comp, "x2"), function(x) x)
```

The estimates follow the truth.
Like any tree-based model, they are step functions, and they flatten towards the edges of the data, where few rows determine them.

The interaction `x1:x3` should look like the product `2 x1 x3`: positive where `x1` and `x3` have the same sign, negative where they differ.

```{r pair, fig.alt = "The x1:x3 component as a scatter of the data coloured by its value: positive where x1 and x3 have the same sign.", fig.height = 4}
autoplot(comp, c("x1", "x3"))
```

## Components of three predictors

A component of three predictors cannot be drawn as one picture.
It is shown as heat maps over two of its predictors, one heat map per interval of the third.
A forest's own three-way component can need hundreds of such heat maps, one for each pair of neighbouring cut points of the third predictor.
So by default (`max_panels = 10`), a kept component that needs more than 10 is coarsened: the third predictor is cut into at most 10 intervals, the component is averaged within each, and the model is pruned again with the coarsened component in place.
Predictions use the coarsened component, so the model that is printed and plotted is the model that predicts.

`model$components` records the form of each component:

```{r forms}
model$components[, c("component", "form", "heat_maps")]
```

and `model$display$coarse` the details of each coarsened one:

```{r coarse}
shown <- model$display$coarse[["x2:x3:x4"]]
shown$C         # the predictor cut into intervals
shown$cuts      # its cut points
shown$var_kept  # share of the component's variance the coarsened form keeps
```

The coarsened component keeps `r round(100 * shown$var_kept)`% of the variance of the forest's component.
Each of its heat maps is over the two other predictors, `setdiff(shown$S, shown$C)`, for the rows whose `x3` lies in one interval.

<!-- TODO(glex): draw the heat maps of x2:x3:x4 once glex draws pruned models (the rpf-pruned branch). -->
The installed glex (version `r packageVersion("glex")`) does not yet draw components of three continuous predictors, so this article does not plot them.

`max_panels = Inf` keeps every component as the forest has it, and the [Pruning](pruning.html) article says more about how the coarsening is chosen.

## Purification

The trees of a forest do not by themselves give unique components.
A main effect of `x1` can sit in trees on `x1` alone or in trees on `x1` together with other predictors.
Purification moves every part of the forest's prediction to the lowest-order component it belongs to, without changing the prediction.

The components are identified by the training data: for every component, its average over the training rows along any one of its predictors is zero, for any value of its other predictors (the marginal identification of Hiabu, Meyer and Wright, 2023; see `?purify`).
The intercept is the mean prediction on the training rows.

`rpf()` purifies the forest while pruning; the pruned model stores its kept components, so you do not need to call `purify()` (and it holds no forest to purify unless fitted with `keep_forest = TRUE`).
For a forest fitted with `prune = FALSE`, `predict_components()` purifies it on first use.
[How the forest is grown](growing.html) shows what purification does to the trees of one family.
